subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 62-year-old woman with a body mass index of 32 has 1 year of increasing knee pain after long walks. The pain improves after she rests and is worse at the end of the day. She has no fever, morning stiffness, or rash. Physical examination shows crepitus and a mild effusion without warmth.
question: Which of the following best characterizes the most likely joint disease?

options.text: Mechanical stress causing cartilage destruction, with pain after use that improves with rest and no systemic symptoms
Autoimmune pannus formation with symmetric morning stiffness lasting longer than 1 hour
Monosodium urate crystal deposition with acute monoarthritis
Septic arthritis with fever and a hot, tender joint
Demyelinating disease causing loss of proprioception

explanation_correct: Osteoarthritis results from chronic mechanical stress that destroys articular cartilage, with inflammation and inadequate repair mediated by chondrocytes. Predisposing factors include age, female sex, obesity, and joint trauma. Pain occurs in weight-bearing joints after use and improves with rest, involvement is asymmetric, and there are no systemic symptoms.

explanation_incorrect.B: That describes rheumatoid arthritis, an autoimmune disease with symmetric involvement, morning stiffness longer than 1 hour that improves with use, and systemic symptoms.
explanation_incorrect.C: That describes gout, an acute inflammatory monoarthritis from monosodium urate crystals.
explanation_incorrect.D: Septic arthritis presents with fever and a hot, tender joint, which is absent here.
explanation_incorrect.E: Loss of proprioception from demyelination does not produce the mechanical, use-dependent joint pain described.

educationalObjective: Recognize osteoarthritis as mechanically driven, use-dependent joint pain without systemic symptoms.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 70-year-old man has progressive right hip pain. Radiography shows osteophytes, asymmetric joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, and cysts. Arthrocentesis yields clear fluid with a white blood cell count of 800/mm3.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this synovial fluid and the underlying process?

options.text: Inflammatory fluid with more than 2000 white blood cells per mm3 from autoimmune pannus
Septic fluid with neutrophils and a positive Gram stain
Noninflammatory fluid with fewer than 2000 white blood cells per mm3 from cartilage loss and osteophyte formation
Fluid containing negatively birefringent monosodium urate needles
Fluid containing positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate rhomboids

explanation_correct: Osteoarthritis is a noninflammatory arthritis; synovial fluid typically has fewer than 2000 white blood cells per mm3. Imaging shows osteophytes, asymmetric joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis and cysts, and loose bodies. These findings reflect chondrocyte-mediated cartilage destruction with inadequate repair.

explanation_incorrect.A: Inflammatory synovial fluid with elevated white blood cells is typical of rheumatoid arthritis, driven by autoimmune pannus.
explanation_incorrect.B: Septic arthritis would show marked neutrophilia and organisms on Gram stain, not clear noninflammatory fluid.
explanation_incorrect.D: Monosodium urate crystals are negatively birefringent needles seen in gout, not osteoarthritis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals are positively birefringent rhomboids seen in pseudogout, not osteoarthritis.

educationalObjective: Know that osteoarthritis has noninflammatory synovial fluid with fewer than 2000 white blood cells per mm3 and osteophytes on imaging.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 66-year-old woman has painless bony enlargements of the distal and proximal interphalangeal joints of both hands and at the base of the thumb. She also has knee pain relieved by rest. She asks about treatment.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this condition?

options.text: Long-term daily intra-articular glucocorticoid injections
Intravenous TNF-alpha inhibitor infusions
High-dose oral methotrexate
Systemic sulfasalazine plus hydroxychloroquine
Activity modification, NSAIDs, and short-term intra-articular glucocorticoids if symptomatic

explanation_correct: These enlargements are Heberden nodes at the DIP joints, Bouchard nodes at the PIP joints, and first carpometacarpal joint involvement of osteoarthritis. Management includes activity modification and NSAIDs, with intra-articular glucocorticoids used for short-term relief in symptomatic patients. Long-term steroid injections are avoided because of adverse effects.

explanation_incorrect.A: Long-term intra-articular glucocorticoid therapy is associated with many adverse effects and is not recommended; steroids are used only for short-term relief.
explanation_incorrect.B: TNF-alpha inhibitors are biologic agents used for rheumatoid arthritis, not osteoarthritis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Methotrexate is a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug used in rheumatoid arthritis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine are DMARDs used for rheumatoid arthritis, not for mechanical osteoarthritis.

educationalObjective: Identify Heberden and Bouchard nodes and choose activity modification, NSAIDs, and short-term intra-articular steroids for osteoarthritis.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 44-year-old woman has 4 months of symmetric pain and swelling in her hands and wrists with morning stiffness lasting 2 hours that improves as the day goes on. She reports fatigue and low-grade fever. Serum testing shows an IgM antibody directed against the Fc portion of IgG, present in about 80% of patients with this condition, and a more specific antibody against citrullinated peptides.
question: Which of the following best describes this patient's disease and its serologic markers?

options.text: Osteoarthritis; rheumatoid factor is usually positive and anti-CCP is more specific
Rheumatoid arthritis; rheumatoid factor is IgM against IgG Fc in 80% and anti-CCP is more specific
Systemic lupus erythematosus; anti-dsDNA is the most specific test
Gout; uric acid crystals are the diagnostic marker
Sjogren syndrome; anti-SSA/SSB antibodies are characteristic

explanation_correct: This is rheumatoid arthritis, an autoimmune disease with female predominance and associations with HLA-DR4, HLA-DRB1, and smoking. Rheumatoid factor is an IgM antibody targeting the Fc portion of IgG and is found in about 80% of patients, while anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody is more specific. Symptoms include symmetric pain and swelling with morning stiffness longer than 1 hour that improves with use, plus systemic symptoms such as fever and fatigue.

explanation_incorrect.A: Osteoarthritis has no systemic symptoms, asymmetric involvement, pain that worsens with use and improves with rest, and is not associated with rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP.
explanation_incorrect.C: Systemic lupus erythematosus can cause arthritis but is associated with anti-dsDNA and other autoantibodies, not rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP as the defining markers.
explanation_incorrect.D: Gout is a crystal arthropathy with monosodium urate crystals and acute monoarthritis, not symmetric chronic polyarthritis with these antibodies.
explanation_incorrect.E: Sjogren syndrome features sicca symptoms and anti-SSA/SSB antibodies; it can coexist with rheumatoid arthritis but does not explain this presentation.

educationalObjective: Associate rheumatoid arthritis with IgM rheumatoid factor against IgG Fc in 80% and the more specific anti-CCP antibody.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 52-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has deformities of both hands. Radiography shows erosions, juxta-articular osteopenia, and symmetric joint space narrowing involving the MCP and PIP joints and wrists. On examination her fingers deviate toward the ulnar side, and several digits show a hyperextended PIP joint with a flexed DIP joint.
question: Which of the following best names the deformities described?

options.text: Heberden nodes at the DIP and Bouchard nodes at the PIP joints
Ulnar deviation with swan neck and boutonniere deformities
Osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and loose bodies
Boutonniere deformity alone with sparing of the MCP joints
Cervical subluxation with ankylosis of the wrists

explanation_correct: Rheumatoid arthritis involves the MCP, PIP, and wrist joints and produces erosions, juxta-articular osteopenia, soft tissue swelling, and symmetric joint space narrowing. Characteristic deformities include ulnar finger deviation, swan neck deformity (hyperextension of the PIP with flexion of the DIP), and boutonniere deformity (flexion of the PIP with hyperextension of the DIP), as well as cervical subluxation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Heberden and Bouchard nodes are osteoarthritis findings at the DIP and PIP joints, not the deformities described in rheumatoid arthritis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and loose bodies are features of osteoarthritis rather than rheumatoid arthritis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Boutonniere deformity is the reverse posture (flexed PIP, hyperextended DIP) and does not account for the ulnar deviation or the described swan neck posture; MCP joints are typically involved.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cervical subluxation can occur in rheumatoid arthritis, but the described finger findings are ulnar deviation and swan neck deformity, and wrist ankylosis is not typical.

educationalObjective: Recognize ulnar deviation, swan neck, and boutonniere deformities as characteristic rheumatoid arthritis hand findings.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 58-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis develops firm subcutaneous nodules over his elbows. Biopsy shows a central zone of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by palisading histiocytes. He also has a history of pneumoconiosis and recently developed progressive dyspnea with basilar crackles.
question: Which of the following best identifies the pathologic basis of these findings?

options.text: Rheumatoid nodules with fibrinoid necrosis and palisading histiocytes; Caplan syndrome when combined with pneumoconiosis
Noncaseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells
IgA deposition within the mesangium
Neutrophilic vasculitis of small vessels
Amyloid deposits showing apple-green birefringence

explanation_correct: Rheumatoid nodules are extra-articular manifestations consisting of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by palisading histiocytes, found in subcutaneous tissue and lung. When rheumatoid arthritis coexists with pneumoconiosis, this is Caplan syndrome. Rheumatoid arthritis can also cause interstitial lung disease, pleuritis, and pericarditis, which may explain his dyspnea.

explanation_incorrect.B: Noncaseating granulomas suggest sarcoidosis, not the fibrinoid necrosis with palisading histiocytes of rheumatoid nodules.
explanation_incorrect.C: Mesangial IgA deposition characterizes IgA nephropathy or Henoch-Schonlein purpura, not rheumatoid nodules or Caplan syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: Neutrophilic small-vessel vasculitis suggests granulomatosis with polyangiitis or another vasculitis, not the palisading histiocytic nodules described.
explanation_incorrect.E: Apple-green birefringence under polarized light indicates amyloid deposition; AA amyloidosis is a complication of rheumatoid arthritis but does not produce these nodules.

educationalObjective: Identify rheumatoid nodules as fibrinoid necrosis with palisading histiocytes and associate their pulmonary form with pneumoconiosis in Caplan syndrome.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 60-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has splenomegaly and recurrent infections. Laboratory studies show anemia, a neutrophil count of 900/mm3, and a platelet count of 95,000/mm3. She has symmetric arthritis of the MCP joints.
question: Which of the following terms best describes this constellation of findings?

options.text: Caplan syndrome
Sjogren syndrome
Felty syndrome (SANTA: splenomegaly, anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, arthritis)
AA amyloidosis
Still disease

explanation_correct: Felty syndrome is a complication of long-standing rheumatoid arthritis characterized by the SANTA mnemonic: Splenomegaly, Anemia, Neutropenia, Thrombocytopenia, and Arthritis (rheumatoid). The neutropenia and splenomegaly predispose to recurrent infections. Other extra-articular features of rheumatoid arthritis include rheumatoid nodules, interstitial lung disease, pleuritis, pericarditis, AA amyloidosis, Sjogren syndrome, scleritis, and carpal tunnel syndrome.

explanation_incorrect.A: Caplan syndrome is rheumatoid arthritis with pneumoconiosis and pulmonary nodules, not the splenomegaly and cytopenias described.
explanation_incorrect.B: Sjogren syndrome features dry eyes and dry mouth with anti-SSA/SSB antibodies, not splenomegaly and neutropenia.
explanation_incorrect.D: AA amyloidosis in rheumatoid arthritis causes proteinuria and renal dysfunction due to serum amyloid A deposition, not this combination of cytopenias.
explanation_incorrect.E: Still disease is a systemic inflammatory disorder with fever, rash, and arthritis, not a complication defined by splenomegaly and cytopenias in rheumatoid arthritis.

educationalObjective: Use the SANTA mnemonic to identify Felty syndrome in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis, splenomegaly, and cytopenias.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 35-year-old woman has had symmetric metacarpophalangeal joint pain and morning stiffness for 4 months. She is positive for anti-CCP antibody. Her physician wants to start therapy that alters disease progression rather than only relieving symptoms.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate disease-modifying treatment?

options.text: Intra-articular glucocorticoids alone
Oral NSAIDs alone
Short-term systemic glucocorticoids alone
A disease-modifying antirheumatic drug such as methotrexate or sulfasalazine
Broad-spectrum antibiotics

explanation_correct: Rheumatoid arthritis treatment includes NSAIDs and glucocorticoids for symptom control, but disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs such as methotrexate and sulfasalazine are used to alter disease progression. Biologic agents such as TNF-alpha inhibitors are also effective. Early DMARD therapy helps prevent erosive joint damage.

explanation_incorrect.A: Intra-articular glucocorticoids are used in osteoarthritis for short-term symptomatic relief and do not modify rheumatoid disease progression.
explanation_incorrect.B: NSAIDs reduce pain and inflammation but do not slow the structural progression of rheumatoid arthritis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Systemic glucocorticoids can control flares but are not disease-modifying and are not used as long-term monotherapy.
explanation_incorrect.E: Antibiotics have no role in rheumatoid arthritis unless a superimposed septic arthritis is present.

educationalObjective: Choose a DMARD such as methotrexate or sulfasalazine to modify rheumatoid arthritis disease progression.
